transcript:
## Introduction: A Nine-Part Series on Anxiety

We're starting this morning a nine-part series on anxiety. The thesis statement, the main point that connects one lesson to the other, is this: **Contrary to what the world and many in the church think, anxiety is a heart or inner man issue best solved by focus on God instead of medical solutions.**

We'll try to show you how knowing and meditating on the attributes of God does the greatest good for the anxious heart.

Throughout this series, anxiety is present everywhere, and I want us to shift from a clinical victim-hood view of anxiety to a godward view of how we can solve anxiety and deal with it. Here's our roadmap: Today we introduce the series. Then we'll look at anxiety in the book of Job. Next, we begin looking at attributes of God and anxiety—the fatherhood of God, the aseity of God (God's self-existence), God's omniscience, God's sovereignty, the love of God, God's omnipresence, and finally the God who answers prayers. As we shift our thinking from anxiety being a medical issue to being a heart issue best solved by turning to God and His attributes, we'll explore who God is.

## The Core Text: Matthew 6:25-34

Let me read what our Lord says in Matthew 6, starting at verse 25:

> Therefore I say to you, do not worry about your life, what you eat or what you drink, nor about your body, what you put on. Is not life more than food and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? Which of you by worrying can add one cubit to his stature? So why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin; yet I say to you that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Now if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will He not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not worry, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For after all these things the Gentiles seek; for your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. Therefore do not worry about tomorrow; for tomorrow will worry about its own things. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. (Matthew 6:25-34)

## Why Anxiety Matters: Four Key Reasons

You may be asking yourself: Why anxiety? Why spend time talking about anxiety, and why spend two months talking about it? Let me give you four reasons why this is important and beneficial to you.

### Reason One: Anxiety Is Everywhere

One in five adults in the United States—about 19% of the population—have been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. Roughly 42.5 million Americans are currently living with anxiety, and nearly one out of three Americans, about 31%, have experienced an anxiety disorder at some point in their lives.

According to psychiatrists and psychologists, there are only four groups that struggle with anxiety: young and old, male and female, Christian and non-Christian, pastors and lay people. So if you're outside of these four groups, anxiety doesn't really affect you.

### Reason Two: Anxiety Has Been Misplaced in the Medical Realm

We live in a time and culture that has misplaced anxiety in the realm of diseases or disorders, and that's not a good thing. The DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Psychiatric Disorders, Fifth Edition) includes 23 different diagnoses related to anxiety: separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder, substance-medication-induced anxiety disorder, anxiety disorder due to another medical condition, and many others including obsessive-compulsive disorder, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania (pulling your hair when anxious), excoriation disorder (skin picking when anxious), major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, personality disorder, and psychotic disorders.

All of these include anxiety as either a cause or a manifestation. We need to talk about it so that we can place it where it belongs. It doesn't belong in the medical sphere—it belongs in the spiritual sphere. That's important for us to see.

### Reason Three: The Bible Has Much to Say About Anxiety

The Bible addresses anxiety extensively, which is what we'll be exploring over the next eight weeks.

### Reason Four: There Is Great Hope for the Anxious Heart

When we view the problem and the solution rightly, there is great hope. When we place the problem in the wrong category, we also get the wrong solution. When we place the problem in the right category, the solution is there, and there's great hope. God's solutions are always much better than any other solution. Offering true hope is the most compassionate thing we can do for anyone with an anxious heart.

## Locating Anxiety: Popular Wisdom vs. Biblical Model

Locating anxiety and putting the origin of anxiety in the right place is very important.

**Popular Wisdom** classifies anxiety as a disorder. The origin is seen as a brain/body disease. The status of the individual is as a helpless victim—something that happens to you. The primary classification is a medical disorder to be treated or accommodated. The prescribed solution is medication and coping mechanisms, maybe some therapy.

**The Biblical Model** sees anxiety as a heart or inner self issue. The status of the individual is as an active responder to the situations of life. The primary classification is as a sanctification issue—an issue of the heart. The prescribed solution is repentance, faith, and a godward focus.

The Bible locates anxiety in the heart. In Proverbs 12:25, the Holy Spirit says:

> Anxiety in the heart of man causes depression, but a good word makes it glad. (Proverbs 12:25)

## The Inner and Outer Man

It will benefit us to revisit what we considered in the morning service when we looked at the inner and outer selves. Remember, we're looking at 2 Corinthians 4:16, where Paul says:

> Therefore we do not lose heart even though our outward man is perishing, yet the inward man is being renewed day by day. (2 Corinthians 4:16)

The outer man is the physical body—our physical bodies are wasting away. The inner man is the immaterial part, our spiritual self, our heart, which can continue to grow and become more alive in Jesus Christ.

The outer man and the inner man are connected, and one affects the other. But physical decline or suffering does not necessitate spiritual decline. Even someone suffering with dementia, which is an outer man or body experience, can be renewed in the inner self because of the Word of God.

Our conclusion is this: **our bodies cannot make us sin.** Whatever the Bible says is sin, we cannot attribute to the physical. Even when our bodies are decaying, we still can be renewed day by day to become more like Jesus Christ.

The outer man affects the inner man, and the inner man affects the outer man, because we are a unit—we're not two separate entities. But it's important to locate things where they are supposed to be.

Because anxiety is a heart issue, the primary way to deal with it is through the heart. And because anxiety is a heart issue, it is not something that happens to us.

**Anxiety is a response of the heart to certain circumstances around us or to inner thoughts.** People and situations don't make us anxious. We respond to people and situations with anxiety as a response of the heart—not something they are doing to us.

## The Two Trees: Jeremiah 17:5-8

Let me read a very important passage. Look at Jeremiah 17, verses 5 through 8:

> Thus says the Lord: "Cursed is the man who trusts in men and makes flesh his strength, whose heart departs from the Lord. For he shall be like a shrub in the desert and shall not see when good comes, but shall inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, a salt land which is not inhabited. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord and whose hope is in the Lord. For he shall be like a tree planted by the waters, which spreads out its roots by the river and will not fear when heat comes; but its leaf will be green, and will not be anxious in the year of drought, nor will cease from yielding fruit." (Jeremiah 17:5-8)

David Powlison, one of those guys worth reading, developed a very helpful way to illustrate how anxiety works. It's based on these two trees we find in Jeremiah 17.

What do we have here? Jeremiah tells us that both trees are under the same sun. They're in the same heat. There's no difference in the environment of the shrub or the fruitful tree. The environment is the same. The context in Jeremiah is judgment for both—it's not like the fruitful tree is in great ease of life while the other suffers. They're both in the same context of judgment.

But one is a dried-up shrub and the other is a fruitful tree.

Both trees are under the same sun, or the same heat. And heat is what happens to you—it's coming from the outside. Yet one is fruitless and shriveled while the other is fruitful and healthy. **What is the difference between the two? It's where their roots reach.** The one is producing fruit under the same sun, under the same circumstances, under the same heat, because the roots are grounded in what brings life. The other tree is facing the same issues in life, but it's a shriveled-up shrub because of where its roots are grounded.

So the problem is not the heat. The problem is not circumstances. The problem is not the people in our lives. **The problem is where we are rooted and where our heart is.** This becomes the issue.

Notice that in verses 5 and 7 of Jeremiah 17, the difference between the two kinds of trees—the two kinds of people—is a heart issue. One of the results of trusting and hoping in the Lord is not being anxious in the year of drought. When all these things are happening, you don't respond in anxiety.

This is important: not being anxious in the year of drought is not trusting God in general. It's trusting God in specific issues. We tend to say, "Yeah, I trust in God," and we do that in an abstract way. But when it comes to specific issues, we forget that general, abstract trust in God.

## Anxiety Is Disobedience to God

We may not be convinced that anxiety is disobedience to God. So follow with me in this logic exercise. Biblically grounded logic: Sin, according to the Scriptures, is either not doing what God commands us to do, or doing what God commands us not to do.

In 1 John 3:4, John says:

> Whoever commits sin also commits lawlessness; and sin is lawlessness. (1 John 3:4)

Sin is not obeying the law of God. A command is a law. God commands us not to be anxious:

> Be anxious for nothing. (Philippians 4:6)

Therefore, **being anxious is a sinful response** to what is going on around us. And brothers and sisters, the purpose of showing you that anxiety is a sinful action of the heart is to point you to Christ through repentance and faith—not to beat you down. You're not going to find relief from anxiety until you see it in its proper place. Because relief from anxiety is only through Christ Jesus and the work of the Spirit.

**Anxiety is a fruit of self-reliance,** even when you are not aware of it. It is an idolatrous desire to control all things and to know all things. Anxiety is idolatrous because it controls you—it becomes what you are worshiping. It's idolatrous because when you're trying to control all things and know all things, you're trying to be God. That's idolatrous.

**By definition, anxiety is an idolatrous response to what happens to us—to the heat of life.**

## Defining Anxiety: When Concern Becomes Sin

The word translated as anxiety or worry in Matthew 6 is not necessarily a negative word in itself. For example, in 1 Corinthians 12:25, the Apostle Paul says:

> That there should be no schism in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. (1 Corinthians 12:25)

The word "care" is the same word as "worry" or "anxiety" in Matthew 6. Or in Philippians 2:20, Paul says:

> For I have no one like-minded who will sincerely care for your state. (Philippians 2:20)

The word "care" is the same word used for anxiety in Philippians 4:6. So the word itself doesn't mean it's inherently bad. But what makes healthy worry or concern move into anxiety, and therefore sin?

Healthy concern becomes anxiety when **any of these things happen**:

1. **Thoughts are focused on changing the future.** Your concern becomes anxiety when you think, "I must change what's going to happen tomorrow." If any of you struggle with OCD-like things, a lot of that is going on here.

2. **Thoughts are unproductive.** You're just thinking about whatever it is that you worried about, spinning there—like the spinning beach ball on an Apple computer that just keeps going forever.

3. **Your worry controls you instead of you controlling it.** If you've been severely anxious, you know exactly what that is.

4. **It causes you to neglect other responsibilities and relationships.** You focus on that one thing, and whatever else God is calling you to do, you don't pay attention to it.

5. **It damages your body.** Remember, the inner man and outer man are connected. Things going on in the inner man can affect your biological and physiological health. We find that with David in Psalm 32, Psalm 51, and Psalm 38, where unconfessed anxiety over his sins made his bones ache.

6. **You lose hope instead of finding answers.** Your concern has become anxiety.

7. **You stop functioning altogether.**

Each one of these things makes healthy concern become anxiety. You can see that in Jesus's admonition for us not to be anxious in Matthew 6.

## Jesus's Solution: A God-ward Orientation

In talking about anxiety, Jesus gives us as a solution a God-ward orientation—not something to do with our body, but something to do with who God is. That's where He points us.

We see in Matthew 6 that Jesus talks about worry. Jesus apparently hasn't read any of the current Christian books on anxiety, because He starts by saying: **"Do not be anxious."** This implies a Holy Spirit ability not to be anxious.

Look at verse 25 of Matthew 6: "Therefore I say to you, do not worry about your life." What's the reason for that? The answer is in verse 26: **Because you are valuable to the Father.**

Jesus makes an argument from the lesser to the greater: If He takes care of the lilies of the field, if He takes care of the grass and the sparrows in the air who are not as important to Him as you are, how much more would He take care of you?

When Jesus says don't worry, what does He point to? **To an attribute of God—His faithfulness to you. You're valuable to Him.**

Look at verse 27: "Which of you by worrying can add one cubit to his stature?" So which one of you can worry so hard that as a result you're either living longer or growing taller? The answer is no one. So **one of the reasons Jesus says don't worry is because it does not accomplish anything.**

Then look at verse 28: "So why do you worry about clothing?" Don't worry because the solution comes from verse 30: "Now if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will He not much more clothe you?" **Don't worry because God cares for you.**

In verse 31, He says don't worry, but instead look to God. In verse 33, He says: **"Seek His kingdom and His righteousness."** Then in verse 34, He says don't worry about what is coming tomorrow because it is a waste of your time.

Have you ever been anxious about a test or about having to talk to somebody tomorrow? You worry and worry and worry, and then you talk to the person, and nine times out of ten, eight times out of ten, seven times out of ten—the experience of talking to the person is much less concerning than the worrying you had all the way leading to it.

Worrying is carrying tomorrow's load with today's strength, gaining two days at once. It is moving tomorrow ahead of time. Worrying does not empty tomorrow of its soil; **it empties today of its strength.** That's what anxiety does.

Notice in verse 30 that **Jesus Himself makes anxiety a matter of faith, not a matter of mental health.** When He says, "O you of little faith," **it's not a mental health issue—it is a heart, a faith issue.**

The Godward orientation of the solution to anxiety in Jesus's teaching goes beyond this one place. For example, in Matthew 10:19-20, He tells us:

> When they deliver you up, do not worry about how or what you should speak. For it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. (Matthew 10:19-20)

We're not to worry about what we should say on God's behalf because the Holy Spirit is in us.

In Luke 10:41, He's talking to Martha and says: "Don't worry about what needs to be done. Instead, focus on Jesus."

When you're anxious about something, your first reaction is to solve that, to focus on that, instead of focusing on what the Lord is doing and what the Lord can do. We tend to push prayer to the side because we're going to solve this issue right in front of us.

**The Godward orientation of the solution to anxiety is also a theme of the Psalms.** In Psalm 94:19, the Psalmist says:

> In the multitude of my anxieties within me, Your comforts delight my soul. (Psalm 94:19)

But our culture today says, "No, no. You got it wrong. You need an anti-depressant. You need something else to solve that—not God, not the comfort of God. You need something else." And a lot of us in the church actually believe that. It's just fool's gold. It doesn't deliver.
